title: Karnataka Demands NEET Abolition as Deputy CM Parameshwara Writes to PM Modi
excerpt: Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara has formally written to Prime Minister Modi seeking the replacement of NEET with state-administered entrance tests, as Karnataka intensifies its challenge to India's centralised medical admissions system amid ongoing paper leak controversies.
body:
• Karnataka Deputy CM G. Parameshwara has written to PM Modi demanding NEET be scrapped and replaced with state-level Common Entrance Tests (CETs)
  • Parameshwara accused Modi of responding "very late" to the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak scandal and called for the dismissal of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan
  • The NEET-UG 2026 exam held on May 3 was cancelled after a massive paper leak; a re-exam was conducted on June 21 for 22.79 lakh students
  • Multiple opposition-ruled states, including Tamil Nadu, have joined Karnataka in demanding the end of the centralised entrance test

Karnataka Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi urging the Centre to abolish the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) and restore the power of states to conduct their own medical entrance examinations. The letter marks the latest escalation in a months-long standoff between several opposition-governed states and the Centre over India's troubled centralised testing system.

Parameshwara, who also serves as the state's Home Minister, launched a scathing attack on the Modi government on Thursday, accusing it of responding "very late" to the NEET paper leak scandal that has thrown the futures of lakhs of medical aspirants into uncertainty. He demanded the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, arguing that those in positions of power must take accountability for the systemic failures.

"This scandal appears to have been orchestrated to enable the sale of MBBS seats, and there are strong suspicions that powerful individuals are behind the entire affair."

— Sharan Prakash Patil, Karnataka Medical Education Minister

A Broken Exam System

The NEET-UG 2026 examination, held on May 3, was cancelled after a massive paper leak was uncovered. According to reports, a "guess paper" containing over 400 questions — including more than 120 matches in Biology and Chemistry — circulated widely on WhatsApp and Telegram groups before the exam. The leak reportedly originated in Nashik, Maharashtra, and spread through networks in Haryana, Rajasthan, Bihar, Kerala, and several other states.

The CBI, which is probing the scandal, has arrested five individuals and blocked over 120 Telegram channels used to distribute the leaked material. A re-examination was conducted on June 21 for the 22.79 lakh registered candidates. Results, declared on July 16, have already drawn legal challenges — a candidate in Madhya Pradesh has moved the High Court alleging a 241-mark discrepancy between his calculated score and NTA's scorecard, while a student from Beed has filed a similar petition in the Bombay High Court.

Karnataka's Case for State-Run Tests

Karnataka Medical Education Minister Sharan Prakash Patil has been among the most vocal critics of the centralised testing regime. At a press conference in Bengaluru, Patil called the paper leak a "grave injustice" to the student community and accused the Centre of "sabotaging" the futures of aspiring doctors.

Patil argued that Karnataka's Common Entrance Test, administered by the Karnataka Examinations Authority (KEA), has a decades-long track record of transparent, merit-based admissions. The CET system, he said, has enabled lakhs of students from rural, middle-class, and economically weaker backgrounds to secure seats in professional courses based on academic performance rather than coaching industry access.

The state government has formally written to the Centre seeking abolition of NEET and permission to conduct admissions through the Karnataka CET system. Patil urged the Union government to "respect the federal structure of the Constitution" and allow states with credible examination mechanisms to run their own entrance tests.

Growing Opposition Chorus

Karnataka is not alone. Tamil Nadu's DMK, which has opposed NEET since its inception, has stepped up its campaign. Former Chief Minister M.K. Stalin wrote to PM Modi in May seeking an ordinance to amend Section 14 of the NMC Act, 2019, to exempt NEET for the 2026-27 academic year and allow states to admit students based on qualifying exam marks. DMK leaders have justified protests outside Parliament, alleging that opposition members are not being allowed to raise the issue inside the House.

"We were the first to warn that NEET was designed to enable large-scale irregularities. That is why the DMK has opposed NEET from the very beginning."

— M.K. Stalin, Former Tamil Nadu Chief Minister

Reform or Repeal?

The Centre has signalled reform rather than repeal. Education Minister Pradhan announced that NEET will shift to a computer-based test (CBT) format from 2027, a move intended to eliminate the paper-leak vulnerability. A high-powered committee headed by former ISRO chairman R. Radhakrishnan is reviewing NTA's processes. On July 1, a parliamentary panel recommended granting statutory status to NTA while raising concerns that the CBT transition could disadvantage students from digitally underserved backgrounds.

For the Indian diaspora, the NEET crisis resonates on multiple levels. Many NRI families send children to India for medical education, and the integrity of the admissions process directly affects trust in the system. The debate also touches on federal governance — whether a vast, diverse country like India is better served by a single national test or by decentralised state examinations that can account for regional curricula and social realities.

With court challenges mounting, opposition states pushing for abolition, and the Centre betting on technological fixes, the future of India's medical entrance system remains deeply uncertain. Parameshwara's letter to Modi is unlikely to change the Centre's stance, but it adds political weight to a growing movement that could reshape how millions of Indian students compete for their shot at a medical career.
